A book by Reem Glasco, LPC-S

Effort-less Self-Care

Effort-less Self-Care: 7 Easy Steps to Calm and Connection is a short daily practice, written by Reem Glasco, LPC-S, for anyone who has been told to look after themselves and found the instruction useless. It takes a few minutes. There is nothing to fix, nothing to achieve, and no way to do it wrong: you sit, you notice what your body is doing, and you name what you find. A companion journal, Reset: 7 Effortless Self-Care Practices to Cultivate Calm and Connection, carries the same seven practices with space to write.

What it asks of you

Noticing, not fixing

Most self-care advice is a list of things to add to a day that is already full. This is the opposite: a practice built on the assumption that your body has been reporting its state all along and nobody taught you to read it.

The seven steps are the clinical work Reem does with clients, reduced to something you can do alone in a chair. They come out of the same lineage as the therapy: Somatic Experiencing, NARM and IFS-informed EMDR, which all start from sensation rather than analysis.

It is not therapy and does not pretend to be. It is a way to arrive at therapy, or at the rest of your day, with better information about what is actually going on.

“Be gentle with yourself. Just breathe.”

The seven steps

  1. Find your comfortable space. Indoors or out, somewhere that invites calm. You might hold a stone, a leaf, a shell. Notice how you feel, and change nothing. Comfort is where healing begins.
  2. Face the light. Sit facing east, toward the morning sun. The direction is doing symbolic work as much as practical: new beginnings. Picture the light on your face. Let the sun guide you.
  3. Return to your heart. Hand on your chest, feel your breath without altering it, for about thirty seconds. Come home to your breath.
  4. Breathe in peace, breathe out stress. Hand still resting there, say softly on the inhale, “I know I am breathing in fresh air,” and on the exhale, “I know I am breathing out stress.” Three times. Breathe in fresh air; breathe out stress.
  5. Pause and feel. Scan from head to toe. Find the tension, the pressure, the ache. Note it; do not fix it. Your body speaks. Listen.
  6. Gently name what you feel. Label the emotion without judgement, then ask what it is trying to tell you, and what is underneath it once the story is set aside. Name it to know it.
  7. Ground yourself through your senses. Still in your spot, hand on your chest, facing east: what do you see, hear, smell, taste, touch? Sit with any shift you feel for at least seventeen seconds. Your senses ground you in the now.

Final reflection

Just breathe

You sat back and observed your inner and outer world, not to fix or analyse it, but simply to notice it. Your breath is always with you: your silent guide.

“You are learning to listen.”

Who it is for

People in or near therapy

Something to do between sessions that builds the same capacity the work builds, without asking you to process anything alone.

Therapists and healers

The Reset journal is written with clinicians in mind: the people who teach regulation all day and practise it least.

Retreat and training groups

The seven steps are the backbone of the mindful trail retreat, where they are practised outdoors rather than in a chair.

Anyone curious about the method

Where the steps come from: NARM, Somatic Experiencing and IFS-informed EMDR, explained in plain language.

Questions about the book

Where can I buy Effort-less Self-Care?

Through Barnes & Noble. It is written by Reem Glasco, LPC-S, a Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor in Texas.

What is the difference between the book and the Reset journal?

Effort-less Self-Care: 7 Easy Steps to Calm and Connection sets out the practice. Reset: 7 Effortless Self-Care Practices to Cultivate Calm and Connection is the self-paced journal that carries the same seven practices with prompts and space to write, aimed particularly at therapists and healers.

How long does the practice take?

A few minutes. Two of the steps have a built-in pause, thirty seconds with a hand on your chest and seventeen seconds of sensory grounding, and the rest take as long as you want to give them. It is designed to survive a bad morning.

Is this a substitute for therapy?

No. It is a daily noticing practice, not treatment, and it is not a crisis resource. If something it surfaces needs more than a journal, that is useful information and a good reason to book a consult.

Do I need to have read it to work with Reem?

Not at all. Clients and supervisees come to the practice without ever having seen it. The book exists for the people who want something to do on their own.

This practice does not provide emergency care. If you are in crisis, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or 911 if you are in immediate danger.
